Elizabeth I. The Queen of England and Ireland from 1558 to 1603, the last Tudor monarch. Her reign, known as the Elizabethan Era, was a period of cultural flourishing that saw the works of Shakespeare and Marlowe, the expansion of English exploration, and the establishment of a stable Protestant Church.

Elizabeth faced several Catholic conspiracies designed to depose her. Most notably, she ordered the execution of her cousin, Mary, Queen of Scots, in 1587 after uncovering the Babington Plot to assassinate her. Even more significant was her military triumph. Her forces defeated the Spanish Armada in 1588, a victory celebrated in her famous speech to the troops at Tilbury. Earlier in her reign, she had established the moderate Protestant Church of England through the Elizabethan Religious Settlement of 1559, settling the religious question that had plagued the nation for decades.

Elizabeth never married and had no children, earning her the title of the Virgin Queen. Her decision to remain single brought an end to the Tudor line. When she died, the succession passed to her cousin's descendants. James I succeeded her, becoming James VI of Scotland before uniting the English and Scottish crowns. Her father had been Henry VIII, who executed her mother Anne Boleyn and declared Elizabeth illegitimate, yet she would live to become England's most celebrated sovereign.
